CAN.story:
From the 1870s until 1997, the Canadian government paid churches to run Indian residential schools, boarding schools that First Nations, Métis and Inuit children were made to attend. About 150,000 children went to them, and the Catholic Church ran more than half. Under a 2006 settlement, former students could claim compensation for sexual and serious physical abuse through the Independent Assessment Process; it received 38,276 claims, and adjudicators awarded $2.14 billion to 23,431 claimants.
In St John's, Newfoundland, the Christian Brothers, a Catholic teaching order, ran the Mount Cashel orphanage. In December 1975, after two Brothers admitted molesting boys, the police chief and assistant chief ordered the detective to end his investigation. References to sexual assault were removed from his report, the Justice Department laid no charges, and four Brothers were moved out of the province. Police reopened the case in 1989 and nine Brothers were convicted. The Hughes Royal Commission, a provincial public inquiry, reported in 1991 that neither the police nor the Justice Department had handled the files normally.

Two priests of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, a Catholic order with missions in the Arctic, left Canada before trial. Fr Eric Dejaeger fled to Belgium in 1995 when he was about to be charged, and lived in Oblate houses there for 16 years despite an international warrant; after he was returned in 2011 he was sentenced to 19 years for 32 offences against Inuit children in Igloolik. Fr Johannes Rivoire left for France in 1993. Canada issued warrants in 1998 and 2022, France refused to extradite him, and he died there in 2024 without trial.

Under the settlement, the records of residential school abuse claims are to be destroyed after 19 September 2027 unless the claimant asks to keep them. Much of what is known about abuse in Canadian institutions comes from inquiries and compensation claims, and some of the accused were never tried in Canada.

IRL.story:
From the 1930s to the 1990s, Catholic religious orders ran more than 250 industrial schools and other institutions for the Irish state, holding over 30,000 children. The Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse, known as the Ryan Commission, reported in 2009 after nine years of work. It found sexual abuse "endemic" in the boys' institutions, most of them run by the Christian Brothers, a teaching order, and found that Department of Education inspections had failed to stop it. The Christian Brothers sued the commission in 2004 to keep their members' names out, and the report names no abusers. A state redress scheme paid about 12,000 people an average of €65,000.

Inquiries into individual dioceses followed. The Ferns report of 2005 found that Bishop Donal Herlihy moved accused priests to other posts for a time and then reinstated them. The Murphy report of 2009 found that four archbishops of Dublin had not told the Gardaí, the Irish police, what they knew, and that the archdiocese had taken out insurance against abuse claims from 1987. The Gardaí themselves had treated priests as outside their remit. In Cloyne, the 2011 report found that nine complaints made after the church adopted reporting rules in 1996 were not passed to the Gardaí, and said the Vatican's response to those rules had allowed bishops to ignore them.

The Norbertine order moved Fr Brendan Smyth between parishes, dioceses and countries, including the United States, without reporting him. At church meetings in 1975 two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy, and their evidence never reached the police. The Irish government's delay in acting on a request from Northern Ireland's police to extradite him led to the fall of the government in 1994. In 1997 he was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children.

In 2024 a state scoping inquiry recorded 2,395 allegations of sexual abuse against 884 alleged abusers at 308 schools run by 42 religious orders, and the government announced a full commission of investigation. More than half of those alleged abusers are dead.

CHL.story:
In 1959 authorities in Siegburg, Germany, issued a warrant for Paul Schäfer for abusing two boys. He fled, and in 1961 he founded Colonia Dignidad, a closed German commune in southern Chile. The colony recruited children from local farms into its free school and clinic. In 1966 a teenager who escaped took refuge at the West German embassy, which sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. Chilean politicians rejected other escapees' accounts in the 1960s because of the colony's ties to those preparing the 1973 coup. After the coup, DINA, the Pinochet dictatorship's secret police, used the colony to hold and torture opponents, as Chile's Rettig Commission reported in 1991. An investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997. Schäfer hid in Argentina until 2005, and in 2006 a Chilean court sentenced him to 20 years for sexually abusing 25 children.

From the 1960s to 2000, children were taken from mainly poor Chilean mothers, some of whom were told their babies had died, and sent for adoption in the United States and Europe, including Sweden. The practice peaked under Pinochet. A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad, and a congressional committee concluded the state was responsible. As of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice.

In the Catholic Church, parishioners reported Fr Fernando Karadima to the archbishop of Santiago in 1984, and Cardinal Errázuriz shelved a church investigation in 2004–05. In 2015 one of his protégés, Juan Barros, was made a bishop. After a Vatican investigator delivered a 2,300-page report, Pope Francis wrote in 2018 that he had made serious errors in judging the situation, and every bishop in Chile offered to resign.

In 2018 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child found the state responsible for grave violations, including sexual abuse, over 40 years in residences of SENAME, the national child protection service.

In 2019 Chile removed the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for prosecution, for child sexual abuse, so old cases can still be brought. No one had been tried for the adoptions abroad by 2023.

PHL.story:
When Clark Air Base, a US military base in Angeles City north of Manila, closed in 1992, the bars around it lost the American soldiers who had been their customers. The same year Manila's mayor, Alfredo Lim, began closing Ermita, the city's main sex-industry district, and many of its businesses moved to Angeles City and took up foreign tourists as customers. In 2025 the US State Department's trafficking report still named Angeles City as places where sex trafficking frequently occurs. It said most foreign offenders come from Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Britain and the United States, and many are already convicted or charged sex offenders at home.

From 2006 the charity International Justice Mission (IJM) worked with police in several Philippine cities, and by 2016 the number of children trafficked for sex in bars and other establishments there had fallen by 79 to 86 percent. Over 2014 to 2017 the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for child sexual exploitation grew more than twelvefold. Parents, relatives or neighbours were paid by buyers abroad to abuse children in front of a webcam. Because the buyers were abroad, 64 percent of the cases taken up by the police anti-trafficking unit in 2017 began with a referral from a foreign police force. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaking money-laundering law, including failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation in the Philippines. In 2024 Europol, the EU police agency, examined chats between about 12,000 buyer accounts and 100 sellers in the Philippines, gathered over 12 years, and sent leads on 197 buyers to 24 countries.

In 2002 the Catholic bishops apologised and said about 200 of the country's 7,000 priests had committed sexual misconduct over two decades. No national inquiry into abuse in church or state institutions has been found.

IJM estimated that 1 in every 100 children in the Philippines was a victim of online sexual exploitation in 2022. The people paying for it live mostly in a few wealthy countries, so finding them depends on police and banks there.

HTI.story:
From 2004 the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti, MINUSTAH, included a contingent of about 950 soldiers from the Sri Lanka Army. In 2007 the UN's internal investigators reported that its members had sexually exploited and abused children frequently, usually at night, at almost every place they were posted. A 2017 Associated Press investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children between 2004 and 2007. Under UN rules only the country that sends peacekeepers can prosecute them, so the UN could only send the accused home. Sri Lanka took back 114 of them, its authorities judged the acts "consensual", and none was jailed.

Haiti has also sent many children abroad for adoption: 13,986 between 2003 and 2022. Most of its orphanages are private and funded from abroad. The charity Lumos found in 2017 that at least US$70 million a year reached about a third of them, that 92 percent of funders were in the United States and 90 percent were faith-based, and that the donations led people to open orphanages and recruit children away from their families. In 2007 one centre was forced to return 47 children it had been holding for adoption after misleading their parents with payments. After the 2010 earthquake, ten American Baptist missionaries were detained while taking 33 children to the Dominican Republic without proper papers; their leader, Laura Silsby, was convicted of arranging illegal travel. In 2019 the government's social welfare agency, after assessing more than 750 orphanages, identified 3,019 children in them as potential trafficking victims.

In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence by armed groups against 566 children in Haiti, up from 41 girls in 2023, and attributed 411 of the cases to the Viv Ansanm gang coalition. The US State Department reported in 2025 that close to half of gang members are children.

Children in Haiti now face sexual violence from gangs, and many still work as restaveks, unpaid domestic servants in other families' homes, where displacement has raised their risk of sexual exploitation.

COD.story:
In 2002 and 2003, during the war in Ituri province in the east, the Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC), an armed group, enlisted children under 15 as soldiers. The International Criminal Court (ICC), which tries people for war crimes when their own country does not, convicted the UPC's leader, Thomas Lubanga, in 2012 of conscripting and using these children; sexual violence against girl soldiers was raised at his trial but not charged. In 2019 the ICC convicted his commander Bosco Ntaganda of crimes including the rape and sexual slavery of child soldiers.

The UN peacekeeping mission sent to the same area was investigated as well. In 2004 the UN's internal investigators found that peacekeepers in Bunia, Ituri's main town, regularly had sex with girls under 18, some as young as 13, in exchange for food or small sums of money. Of 72 allegations, six were fully substantiated, largely because most reports were too vague to investigate. Peacekeepers can only be prosecuted by the country that sent them, and in a 2025 UN report few cases had been finalised. During the 2018–2020 Ebola outbreak in North Kivu and Ituri, aid workers arrived in the same region. An independent commission appointed by the World Health Organization found in 2021 that WHO staff and other responders, mostly local temporary hires, had used offers of jobs to obtain sex, and that the youngest of those it heard was a 13-year-old girl.

The fighting has continued. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 358 girls in the DRC, by the M23 rebel group, the CODECO militia, the national army and others, and the abduction of 815 children. In the eastern mines, the US State Department reported in 2025, mining bosses, family members, officials and armed groups force children into labour, and girls are trafficked for sex and forced marriage.

In eastern DRC, armed groups and the army continue to abuse and abduct children, and few of the commanders, soldiers or responders accused have been tried. No representative survey has measured online sexual exploitation of children in West and Central Africa, which includes the DRC.

GRC.story:
After the Greek civil war, between 1950 and 1975, as many as 4,000 Greek-born children were adopted by families in the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden. Many were described as orphans of the war or had been born to unmarried mothers, and they came from state institutions and foundling homes. AHEPA and other US agencies and intermediaries arranged the adoptions, often quickly and sometimes by proxy, with the adoptive parents not present in Greece. The adoptions were kept confidential, and many adoptees grew up without papers showing where they came from. The Greek state promised an investigation in the late 1950s and never carried it out. On 2 May 2025 a law recognised the adoptees' status, restored a path to Greek citizenship and made it easier for them to see their records.

Greece's own institutions have also been examined. In 2011 the Greek Ombudsman, an official who investigates complaints against public bodies, found that at the state care centre for disabled children at Lechaina, a shortage of staff had led to systematic sedation, children tied to beds and the use of wooden cage beds. In 2014 the BBC found conditions had barely improved. No finding of sexual abuse there was located.

In its 2025 trafficking report, the US State Department said unaccompanied migrant children in Greece are vulnerable to sex trafficking, and that Roma children from Albania, Bulgaria and Romania are forced to beg there.

The adoptees can now reclaim Greek citizenship. The investigation promised in the 1950s has still not taken place, and no wider inquiry into abuse of children in Greek institutions was found.

DNK.story:
In May 1951 the Danish government, working with Save the Children Denmark, asked teachers and priests in Greenland, then a Danish colony, to pick out children aged six to ten. Twenty-two Inuit children were sent to foster families in Denmark to be brought up as "little Danes". About a year and a half later 16 were returned to Greenland and placed in a children's home built by the Danish Red Cross, and many never lived with their families again; six were adopted in Denmark. A 2020 report found that half of them later had mental health problems. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised in December 2020, and in 2022 the six survivors were each awarded 250,000 kroner.

Denmark's state children's homes were examined in the Godhavn Report of 2011, which covered Godhavn boys' home and 18 other homes from 1945 to 1976. It found neglect and physical and sexual abuse, and that about 22 percent of Godhavn's boys had been given psychiatric drugs by a psychiatrist. No prosecutions followed, and Frederiksen apologised in 2019.

Denmark has also received many children from abroad, including 9,297 from South Korea between 1965 and 2008. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found that agencies there had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign demand and had registered children with known parents as orphans. Denmark suspended adoptions from Ethiopia in 2016 after abuses there, and in 2024 the Danish International Adoption agency, the country's only intercountry adoption agency, said it was closing.

Danish police have led or joined several international investigations of online abuse, from the Bamse bulletin board in the early 1990s to Operation Cumberland in 2025, one of the first cases of AI-generated abuse material, in which 273 suspects were identified.

The children removed from Greenland and the boys in state homes have received apologies, and the Greenlanders compensation. With its only agency closing, Denmark's part in intercountry adoption is ending.
